analysis.one_liner: Sets minimum consumer protections for managed care health plans, including choice of doctor, emergency coverage, appeals, and the right to sue.
analysis.headline: The Health Care Consumer Protection Act of 1997, with 31 House cosponsors from both parties, never received a committee vote or floor vote and died when Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have written federal standards into managed care plans: patients could choose and change their own doctor, plans would have to offer an option to go outside the provider network, emergency care would be covered without prior approval, women could see an OB-GYN directly, and patients with serious illness could get coverage for approved clinical trials. It would also require plans to run fair appeal processes, ban contract clauses that stop doctors from telling patients about treatment options, and let patients sue in state court for injuries caused by a plan's decisions. The bill never came up for a vote in any committee.
analysis.who_benefits: People enrolled in HMOs and other managed care plans, including Medicare and Medicaid managed care patients. The bill would have guaranteed access to emergency rooms without a plan's advance approval, direct access to obstetricians and specialists, continuity of treatment when a provider leaves the network, coverage of routine costs in approved clinical trials, a clear appeals process with independent external review, and the right to sue a plan in state court for personal injury or wrongful death. Doctors and other providers would also gain protections against discriminatory network exclusion and sudden termination.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Managed care enrollees and their doctors

how_it_helps.text: Requires plans to cover emergency services 24 hours a day, seven days a week without prior authorization when a prudent layperson would judge the symptoms an emergency, and to pay for screening and stabilizing services even at out-of-network hospitals [S2][S3].
Requires every plan that only covers network providers to also offer a point-of-service option for out-of-network care, with state-regulated premiums and disclosed cost-sharing [S2][S3].

Lets enrollees pick and change their own doctor, designate an OB-GYN as primary care provider without prior authorization for routine gynecological and pregnancy care, and keep coverage with a treating provider through hospitalization, pregnancy, or terminal illness when the provider leaves the network [S2][S3].

Bars plans from discriminating against patients for joining an approved clinical trial when they have a life-threatening illness with no effective standard treatment, and requires coverage of routine patient costs in trials funded by NIH, VA, or DoD [S2][S3].

Creates a two-stage internal appeal process with strict deadlines and independent external review of denials of experimental therapy for terminal patients and other serious decisions, with the plan paying the review costs [S2][S3].

Nullifies contract clauses that prohibit doctors from discussing treatment options, utilization review requirements, or financial incentives with patients, and imposes civil money penalties for violations [S2][S3].

Amends ERISA so patients can bring state court lawsuits for personal injury or wrongful death against plans and the companies that administer them, ending the federal shield that generally blocks such suits today [S2][S3].

Requires plans to disclose premiums spent on administration versus patient care, provider financial incentives to limit care, utilization review rules, and how often reviewers overrule treating doctors [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and managed care organizations bear the cost of broader coverage mandates, quality programs, disclosure, appeals, and litigation exposure; employers sponsoring group plans, including self-insured plans, would face the new standards and new liability under ERISA; some of these costs would pass through to premiums.

drawbacks.text: The mandates would raise the cost of coverage: an out-of-network point-of-service option, guaranteed emergency coverage without prior approval, and expanded appeals all add claims the plan must pay, and those costs show up in premiums and employer contributions [S2][S3].

Opening ERISA plans to state court damage suits for personal injury or wrongful death would expose employers and plan administrators to new litigation risk, which independent analyses of comparable proposals warned could push more employers to drop coverage or self-insure [S2][S3].

The bill imposes heavy administrative requirements on every issuer, including detailed disclosure of plan economics, provider profiling, and credentialing procedures, which critics of the 1997-1998 managed care debate argued would burden small plans and add to regulatory costs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The patient protections address real, documented practices of 1990s managed care: emergency care denied for lack of pre-approval, doctors barred from telling patients their options, and denials with no independent appeal. The genuine costs are higher premiums, especially from the out-of-network option and the new right to sue, and the bill applies an extensive rulebook uniformly to all plans, large and small. On balance, most of the provisions target cases where a plan's cost control harmed a patient's health, and the cost of those specific protections is comparatively modest; the liability expansion is the most contested part.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees, sent to three subcommittees, and then sat without a hearing, a markup, or any vote until the 105th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Frank Pallone introduced the bill on November 9, 1997, with 31 cosponsors, 26 Democrats and 5 Republicans [S1][S3][S4].
The Speaker referred it to three committees at once: Commerce, Ways and Means, and Education and the Workforce, each to consider only the parts in its jurisdiction [S5].

In late November and early December 1997 it was sent to the Commerce Subcommittee on Health and Environment, the Ways and Means Subcommittee on Health, and the Education and Workforce Subcommittee on Employer-Employee Relations [S5].
No further action appears in the record: no hearings, no committee votes, no floor action, through the end of the Congress on January 3, 1999 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and managed care companies, which avoided new coverage mandates, appeal requirements, disclosure rules, and state-court lawsuits under ERISA; employers with self-insured health plans also avoided the added liability.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers and managed care companies

for.name: Rep. Frank Pallone Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded its referral to three committees.

for.name: 31 House cosponsors (26 Democrats, 5 Republicans)
for.role: Cosponsors including Reps. Gilman, Fox, Horn, McCollum, and Morella
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it support from both parties.

against.name: House committee leadership of the 105th Congress
against.role: Chairs of the Commerce, Ways and Means, and Education and the Workforce Committees
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after its referral, so it never reached a committee or floor vote.

against.name: Health insurance and managed care industry
against.role: Insurers and managed care organizations subject to the bill's mandates
against.what_they_did: Opposed the wave of federal managed care regulation proposed in 1997-1998, including point-of-service mandates and the expansion of liability under ERISA.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan in form, 26 Democrats and 5 Republicans, but the bill never reached a vote; the three committees it sat in were controlled by Republicans, and no recorded vote exists to measure party support.

industries.industry: Health insurers and managed care organizations
industries.note: The bill would impose coverage mandates (emergency care, out-of-network option, clinical trials, direct OB-GYN access), fair appeals, detailed disclosure, and exposure to state court suits. Its cost-control and incentive structures would be directly restricted; the industry's gain under the status quo came from limiting exactly the care and information this bill guaranteed to patients.

industries.industry: Employers with self-insured and ERISA health plans
industries.note: Employees' benefits would gain protections, but employers and plan administrators would face new compliance duties and, under the ERISA amendment, state-court liability for personal injury or wrongful death. That liability risk was the core business objection to bills like this one.

industries.industry: Physicians and other health care providers
industries.note: Providers gain nondiscrimination protections in network selection, due process before termination, an end to 'termination without cause' clauses, and the right to communicate freely with patients about treatment options. Patients' access to care and doctors' freedom from plan interference run together here.

industries.industry: External and independent medical review organizations
industries.note: The bill requires plans to fund external independent review of disputed denials, creating work for certified independent review organizations at plan expense rather than patient expense.
